summary: Vite is a build tool split into a dev server and a Rolldown-based production build. Nearly all of it lives in packages/vite/src/node, with a browser-side HMR client and a module runner beside it. The largest directory is not source at all: playground holds hundreds of small apps used as end-to-end fixtures.

districts.name: The Works
districts.purpose: The published packages: the vite core (dev server, build, plugins, optimizer), the create-vite scaffolder and plugin-legacy.

districts.name: Proving Grounds
districts.purpose: Hundreds of miniature applications, one per feature, driven as end-to-end tests of the real dev server and build.

districts.name: Knowledge District
districts.purpose: The VitePress documentation site: guides, the config reference, the blog and the migration notes.

districts.name: Release Yard
districts.purpose: Release plumbing: changelog extraction, version preparation and the publish steps CI runs.

districts.name: Civic Offices
districts.purpose: Thirteen workflows covering CI, releases, security scanning and a large amount of issue triage automation.

districts.name: The Patchworks
districts.purpose: Three pnpm patches applied to dependencies the project needs to change before use.

importantModules.role: The published vite package: the dev server and its plugin container, the Rolldown build, dependency pre-bundling, the HMR client, module runner, CLI and types.
The npm create vite scaffolder and the framework starter templates it copies, one pair per framework in JavaScript and TypeScript.
The CSS fixture: Sass, Less, Stylus, SugarSS and PostCSS, CSS modules and composes, @import resolution, code splitting, Lightning CSS and minification.
The dependency pre-bundling fixture, with dozens of local packages covering CommonJS, browser-field and ESM interop shapes.
The prose documentation: features, build, SSR, dependency pre-bundling, the plugin and environment APIs, and the migration guide.
Emits a SystemJS chunk and a polyfill chunk alongside every build chunk, so output runs in browsers without native ESM or import.meta.
The hot module replacement fixture: accepted exports, circular dependencies, file delete and restore, and nested dependency updates.
The web worker fixture: classic, module and shared workers, nested and self-referencing workers, and the es and iife worker output formats.
The module resolution fixture: exports and imports fields, the browser field, custom conditions and main fields, extensions, directories and file URLs.
The static asset fixture: asset URLs under relative, encoded, URL and runtime bases, import.meta.url references, public files and the build manifest.
The same accept, invalidate, circular-dependency and delete-restore cases as playground/hmr, run through the module runner instead of the browser.
Root manifest of the @vitejs/vite-monorepo workspace, carrying the lint, typecheck and docs scripts and the unit, serve and build test commands CI runs.
The HTML fixture: several entry pages, inline and async scripts, link props, env substitution, importmap ordering and malformed markup.
The release announcement posts, one per major release from Vite 2 to Vite 8 plus the notable minors, as published on vite.dev.
The server-side rendering fixture for externalised dependencies: CJS interop, nested externals, module conditions and forwarded exports.
The contributor guide: pnpm workspace setup, why most dependencies go in devDependencies because Rolldown pre-bundles them, debugging and running the suites.
The plugin-legacy fixture: SystemJS output, polyfill chunks, modern-target builds, custom filenames and the no-polyfill variants, one vite config each.
The JavaScript sourcemap fixture, covering maps from optimized dependencies, plugin-generated maps, class fields and malicious sourcemap paths.
The server.fs fixture: which files inside and outside the project root the dev server will serve, and which the allow and deny lists must refuse.
The option-by-option config reference, split into shared, server, build, preview, worker, SSR and dependency optimisation pages.
The import.meta.glob fixture: eager and lazy globs, glob arrays sharing a common base, and globs that reach outside the project root.
The dynamic import fixture: variable and aliased paths, nested and self-importing chunks, CSS pulled in by a dynamic chunk, and imports from a local package.
One page per behaviour change being rolled out, including per-environment APIs, the hotUpdate hook and SSR through the module runner.
Runs the playground applications as end-to-end tests across serve, build and bundled-dev modes, carrying the per-mode exclusion lists.
Names the three published packages and rewrites the create-vite template manifests to the new vite version during a release.
The unit test config: every __tests__ spec outside playground, with aliases mapping vite subpath imports back to source.

strengths: Dev and build share one plugin contract through pluginContainer, so a plugin written once behaves the same in both modes.
The end-to-end suite is the product: playground runs real applications against the real server instead of mocking the pipeline.
The public API is explicit, with index.ts and internalIndex.ts separating what is supported from what is internal.
Documentation is a first-class directory with guides, a full config reference and migration notes for each breaking change.
Thirteen workflows cover CI, release, security scanning and the ecosystem CI that tests downstream frameworks.
concerns: packages/vite/src/node is a wide flat directory of roughly 25 top-level files plus server, plugins, ssr and optimizer, so the core has no obvious reading order.
playground is the largest directory in the repository by a wide margin, which makes the tree hard to skim and the test suite expensive to run.
Both the dev server and the production build live in one package, so anything published moves the whole tool at once.
